title: Hosted API: concurrent-retry + KV eviction caused transient 5xx surge during customer escalation
creator: Thomas Nguyen
description: Summary: During a customer escalation, we observed a short-lived but high-volume wave of 5xx and timeout errors from the Hosted API. Root cause investigation points at an interaction between our retry orchestration (proxy+client backoff jitter) and a change in KV cache eviction heuristics leading to repeated cache misses, upstream worker pressure, and concurrent retries (a retry amplification effect). This ticket captures the investigation timeline, immediate mitigations, permanent fixes, rollout plan, and customer communications.
incident_timeline: 2026-02-14 07:42 UTC: First alert - elevated 5xx rate for tenant 'acme-pro'. 07:45: Pager triggered, SRE and on-call runtime engineers joined. 07:50: Initial mitigation - raised proxy circuit-breaker thresholds for the tenant and disabled aggressive global retry ramp. 08:10: Observed partial recovery followed by second spike at 08:22. 09:30: Confirmed correlation between heavy KV cache churn on the ensemble serving nodes and the spike. 11:10: Applied a targeted in-flight request cap per-tenant on the request combiner to stop amplification; 11:25: error rate dropped to baseline. 13:00: Post-incident review started; began work on permanent mitigations and changelist for runtime/serving and proxy components.
investigation_notes: Key signals: a) sudden increase in KV cache eviction rates on a subset of GPU workers; b) corresponding jump in upstream request latency and 502/504s; c) proxies continued retrying with default retry policy and near-synchronous jitter patterns, causing multiple in-flight retries to accumulate; d) tenant 'acme-pro' traffic had a skewed token length distribution leading to longer per-request execution time which amplified queueing. Traced logs show cache miss -> slow path kernel selection -> longer latency -> proxy retry -> new request misses again due to eviction window -> loop. Memory pressure on a small set of workers caused eviction thresholds to trigger more aggressively after a recent autoscaling policy tweak. We reproduced locally by simulating a high variance token length workload with small worker memory buffers and default proxy retry settings.
root_cause_summary: A confluence of changes: (1) subtle change in cache eviction heuristic that reduced KV retention under memory churn on some worker pools; (2) tenant traffic characteristics produced longer-running requests increasing the chance of eviction between initial request and retry; (3) proxy retry scheduling produced correlated retries across clients (insufficient randomized backoff/jitter), resulting in in-flight retry amplification; (4) autoscaler oscillation on a small worker subset prevented quick capacity stabilization. The combined effect produced a transient surge of concurrent work on specific workers that returned 5xx/timeouts to clients.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Applied per-tenant in-flight concurrency caps on the request combiner to bound amplification (rolled forward at 11:10 UTC). 2) Temporarily increased KV cache retention window on affected worker pools to avoid eviction during short retry windows. 3) Tuned proxy to add jitter to retry timings and added an emergency cooldown per-tenant to prevent immediate retry storms. 4) Contacted customer success to notify affected customers and provided ETA for full fix. These measures restored baseline by ~11:25 UTC.
permanent_fix_plan: Short term (1-2 weeks): a) Introduce adaptive per-tenant concurrency quota and backpressure that accounts for observed median latency and token length distribution. b) Adjust KV cache eviction policy to prefer retention for recently-accessed prefix/kv entries when retry probability is high. c) Update proxy retry policy to use exponential backoff with decorrelated jitter and tenant-aware cap. Medium term (3-8 weeks): d) Add a token-length aware scheduler in the batcher to limit head-of-line blocking from long requests. e) Autoscaler fix to dampen oscillations by using longer smoothing windows and cross-pool coordination. Long term: f) Add a simulation harness for combined KV + retry dynamics so we can run chaos tests before tuning policies in production.
rollout_strategy: Phased rollout: 1) Implement proxy retry policy change behind a feature flag; enable for 10% of traffic for 48 hours with tight telemetry. 2) Deploy per-tenant in-flight caps to a staging fleet, then to a small subset of tenants in prod, monitoring error-rate, latency p50/p95, and dropped requests to ensure no regressions. 3) KV eviction heuristic adjustments will be deployed to a canary pool first and observed for cache hitrate and memory stability. 4) All changes gated by automated SLO checks; rollback paths defined in rollout docs.
qa_and_validation: Unit tests for the modified eviction heuristic and proxy retry library. Integration tests that replay recorded 'acme-pro' traffic on a 5-node staging cluster with slow-path kernel traces. Load tests to ensure per-tenant caps do not cause headroom starvation for other tenants. Observability: new dashboards tracking retry amplification ratio, per-tenant in-flight counts, cache hit/miss delta around retries, and worker memory churn. Canaries will run traffic replays for 48h with alert thresholds.
customer_communication: A short incident summary sent to affected customers within 2 hours summarizing impact and mitigations. Follow-up communication promises a technical postmortem and ETA for permanent fixes within 5 business days. Customer success will offer assisted migration to a dedicated capacity pool for customers requiring stricter isolation while fixes roll out. Template messages and Slack threads are attached to this ticket.
follow_up_actions: 1) Postmortem doc + timeline (deliverable: 2026-02-22). 2) Implement simulation harness for retry+cache interactions (owner: Runtime team). 3) Add per-tenant QoS thresholds to Console and expose an alerting rule for customers. 4) Run chaos test on staging to validate eviction/backoff behavior before next major release. 5) Revisit autoscaler smoothing windows and implement coordination across worker pools.
notes: Do not conflate this with previous retry storms that were purely client-driven; this one has a clear server-side component (kv eviction + autoscaler feedback).
Consider whether tenant-specific default retry caps should be available as a Console toggle for customers who are sensitive to transient 5xx spikes.
We simulated the failure locally by driving a high variance token-length workload and reducing worker kvcache buffer size to recreate eviction window behavior.
